s10.slug: THURSDAY · 1:05 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — MISS BROUSSARD TEACHES
body: At ten past two last night the light was still on under the kitchen door on two. He knows because he was on the stairs at ten past two, and the hot oil came up the stairwell to meet him, and he went on up past the landing with his hand on the rail and didn’t knock; the sign on that door has his name on it.

The rain that came through at dawn has left the windows of 302 beaded and the quad below them shining, and somebody has opened the middle one a hand’s width, so the room is cool and the radiator has nothing to argue with. In Morro this morning Skye said *hi* across Pair 41 and then took notes on the tides in green ink for seventy-five minutes, and that was all of her. Fenner did not follow up twice.

Hale has taken Lena’s chair at the window end, as threatened. He sits in it with his legs crossed and *Brideshead* shut on his knee and the fountain pen uncapped and nothing to write on, and Lena stands at the window behind his shoulder with her book open on one palm, so that to see her he has to turn round in his own seat. He keeps turning round.

Her sleeves are shoved to the elbows. At a podium that means she’s about to take somebody apart; here, with a paperback on her palm and the rain light coming off the quad onto one side of her face, it seems to mean only that she is having the time of her life and would rather die than say so.

She’s very good. Jack has watched her take a floor and take this table, every Monday and Thursday since January, and this is neither one: she isn’t arguing, she’s asking. She asks the table things she doesn’t know the answer to, and waits, and lets the sophomores be wrong out loud without rescuing them, and when somebody is right she says so and moves on before they can enjoy it. It is the least Hale-like hour anybody has ever spent in Hollis 302, and Hale, three feet from it, can’t stop turning round to watch.

“Sebastian tells Charles he believes in the star and the three kings,” she says, “because it’s a lovely idea. And Charles says you can’t believe a thing because it’s lovely. And Sebastian says, but I do, that’s how I believe.” She looks down the oak. “Is that a bad reason? I don’t know. I’ve been trying to decide since Sunday.”
Hale twists in the chair. “You don’t *know*?”
“No, Professor. That’s why I asked the table.” She turns a page. “You can tell me afterward, if you’re sure.”

The nose ring says it’s the worst reason there is; it’s how people end up believing in horoscopes. The sophomore beside her says it’s the only reason anybody believes anything, they just dress it up afterward in footnotes. Yusuf says his grandmother believes in the evil eye because it’s a *terrible* idea, and asks whether that’s better or worse, and nobody knows, and Lena points her pencil at him like he’s won a raffle. When the nose ring tells her flatly that she’s wrong about Julia, Hale turns round the other way in his chair to look at the nose ring, only look, and the nose ring withdraws the remark. Caleb has his pen capped on his book again, and Lena leaves him be.
“Sebastian isn’t a fool,” Lena says. “He’s the only person at Oxford who suspects a lovely idea might be lovely because it’s true. And he’s terrified of what it’ll cost him if —”
“Yes,” Hale says.
She stops.
“Yes. That is the book. Go on.”
He has interrupted every person at this table since January, most of them inside their first clause, and never yet to agree with one. Two of the sophomores look at each other. Lena goes on.

She takes them through the end of Book One: the summer over, Charles going back up to Oxford, Sebastian drinking alone in his rooms and lying about it, the happiness already being buried somewhere for later. “It’s a love story,” she says. “Whatever else it is. Book One is a love story.”
Hale doesn’t turn round this time. “Miss Broussard, everything is a love story to someone who’s just won something.”

The table laughs, the sophomores loudest; at the door end Jack keeps his face exactly where it was, which takes some doing. Lena lets it land. She looks at nobody — not Hale, not the door end, a knot in the oak halfway down — and when the laugh has run out she turns a page and goes on as if he’d remarked on the rain.
With ten minutes left she looks down the length of the table to the door end, to him.
“Why does Sebastian need the bear?”

response: Lena turns to the table with it. “Mr. Costigan says because it can’t leave.”
Down the side of the oak Caleb looks up from his capped pen for the first time all week, at Jack, and down again. By then Lena is already asking the nose ring whether Charles can.
“Mr. Costigan has read ahead,” Hale says, before she can.
“Mr. Costigan has read the *back cover*.”
The table enjoys it, Hale most of all. Lena turns a page and doesn’t look at the door end, and the corner of her mouth is doing something she will not let it finish.

choices.text: “Because it’s the only thing at Oxford he doesn’t have to explain himself to.”
response: She doesn’t give that one to the table. She looks at him across the oak for exactly as long as it takes the table to notice, and then turns to Yusuf and asks him about Julia.

At her elbow Hale opens his *Brideshead* for the first time all hour and writes in it. Lena stands at the window with her back to the room for the length of Yusuf’s answer, looking out at the wet quad.

s10a.slug: THURSDAY · 4:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT DESK — FAVE
body: Marcus is on the front desk with his hood up and his orgo open in front of him to a page of hexagons, and on the shelf behind him, between a Zappos box and somebody’s red Netflix envelope, there is a shoebox wrapped in a Giant Eagle grocery bag and taped round and round like a crime scene. Jack would know the hand on it in the dark. It has been on every Easter envelope he ever got, with a five-dollar bill folded in quarters inside and a holy card on top of the five so he’d see the saint first.

body.title: A shoebox in a Giant Eagle bag, Priority Mail
body.text: MISS LENA BROUSSARD · DELGATO HALL · ROOM 217 · from C. RINALDI, GLENWOOD AVE., YOUNGSTOWN, OHIO

body: Nonna’s capitals go uphill and come down hard, every letter a fence post driven in by somebody who learned to write from nuns with rulers and has never seen the point of joining anything up. Priority Mail, Monday’s postmark, from the post office on Glenwood where she still goes in person to buy one stamp at a time.
“That’s my grandmother,” Jack says.
Marcus looks at the box, and at him. “It says Broussard, man.”
“It’s my grandmother’s handwriting.”

“It’s Broussard’s box.” He lifts it off the shelf to show Jack the name, as a courtesy, and it rattles: a dry, small, many-voiced sound, a maraca somebody was too polite to shake. Beans. A shoebox of dried beans, from Ohio. “I buzzed 217 when it came,” Marcus says. “Twenty minutes ago.” He puts it back on the shelf and sits down in front of it.
“I could sign for it.”
“You could sign for your *own* stuff.”

The stairwell door bangs open. Lena comes across the lobby at a dead run in her socks, her hair coming down out of its pencil, and reaches past Marcus’s head and takes the box off the shelf, and puts it behind her back with both hands.
“You didn’t see this.”
“It’s from my grandmother.”
“It’s from *Nonna*,” she says. “That’s a different thing.”
She backs away to the stairwell with the box behind her, rattling at every step, and goes up two at a time.
Marcus watches the door until it stops moving. He turns a page of hexagons. “Your grandma spells it with a T.”
Jack laughs out loud, alone in the middle of the lobby with his bag still on his shoulder, and can’t stop, and Marcus waits him out with the patience of a man who is paid by the hour.

s11.slug: THURSDAY · 7:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE CROSS CAN WAIT
body: The sun is down behind the hills but the sky hasn’t heard yet, and the doors of St. Brendan’s are propped open on the last of the light. On the left-hand door, under the Mass times, there’s a sheet of paper in Father Osei’s slow upright hand.

body.title: Taped to the door of St. Brendan’s
body.text: STATIONS TONIGHT (THURSDAY). TOMORROW IS A SOLEMNITY. —G.O.

body: Inside, the forty are the forty, on the wrong night: the old man with his own kneeling pad, the three nursing students still in scrubs from a late lab, the Knights in their windbreakers, the woman who sits by the third station all evening so she won’t have to walk to it. Lena is already in his pew when he gets there, which has never happened, lace on, booklet open on her palm. When he sits he sees flour in the crease of one knuckle, and when she turns a page there is anise on the air between the pews, faint, under the candle wax. Her eyes have the look they get at the end of a double at the Anchor. He doesn’t ask.
Father Osei comes down the aisle behind the cross in the purple stole and goes up to the ambo before the first station, and looks out at them over the book.
“Tomorrow is St. Joseph,” he says. “The cross will wait one day; it is used to waiting.”
A laugh goes along the pews, low, the kind a church allows itself. Five Fridays in, and this one on a Thursday.

It throws everybody a little. The old man with the kneeling pad starts toward the first station before Gus has given the chord, and stops, and looks up at the loft for permission. One of the nursing students has brought a Friday’s worth of Kleenex. Jack’s knees know this tile by now; they don’t know it on a Thursday, and they tell him so at the first station and the second.

Gus gives the chord from the loft and they go down the south wall and up the north, singing between the carvings, *Let me mingle tears with thee, / mourning him who mourned for me*, the forty a little behind the organ and Lena a little ahead of the forty. Her lips go a half-beat before the responses at every station. She knows them better than the book does.

The thirteenth is near the back, where the light from the doors doesn’t reach. *Jesus is taken down from the cross.* Two men on ladders in the carving, and a sheet, and the body coming down into his mother’s lap as if she had held out her arms for a parcel and been handed this. Father Osei reads it short, his eyes on the page: that they took him down, and gave him to her, and she held what they gave her. Then he lets the church kneel.

Jack kneels on it. *Keep her*, he says, without saying who, and it’s Ma at the sink on Glenwood, and it’s the lace a foot from his shoulder, and he doesn’t sort out which, and the forty stand him back up.

Afterward the steps are cool and the town below has its lights on. Over the hills behind the olive tree a crescent moon is going down, thin as a bead of solder. People come out past them doing up their jackets. She comes down two steps ahead of him and turns round.

Father Osei is at the door behind them, taking hands, being told by the old man with the kneeling pad that Thursday felt wrong. When it’s Jack’s turn he holds on to the hand a little and says, “Tomorrow, Jack, wear a clean shirt.”
Beside Jack, Lena says, “*Father*.”
“It is only advice about shirts,” Father Osei says, and gives his hand to the next person, delighted with himself.
“Go to bed, Costigan,” Lena says. “I’ve got bread.”
She goes down Ocean Road toward the harbor at a walk that wants to be a run, and twice it nearly is, and twice she reins it in.

He sits down on the top step. At the bottom of the hill the Anchor is lit the way it always is, the neon anchor and the booths along the window and Gloria’s counter; and then one more light comes on, a small square at the back by Rudy’s ovens, the window that is dark every night he has ever worked a shift. He stays where he is with his elbows on his knees, the crescent going down by degrees over the ridge, and watches that one window.

s12.slug: FRIDAY · 12:01 AM · DELGADO HALL, HIS STEP — NINETEEN
body: The tube light over the fourth-floor door has the stairwell to itself. Jack is on his step, third down from four, in the Carhartt over a T-shirt and his socks, with the RAZR open on his knee and its little screen the brightest thing on the concrete. He came out at half past eleven for no reason he could have given Theo, and has been watching the minutes go over ever since like a kid watching the odometer on the Turnpike, waiting for all the nines.

The stairwell carries on as before. The light buzzes. Somewhere on three a toilet runs and stops. He’s nineteen, and it feels a great deal like eighteen with the lights off, and he is thinking about getting up.

He has been told not to see so many things this week that he could open a museum of them. A legal pad with nothing on it. A walk-in with her in it. A sign on the kitchen door with his name in Laney’s capitals. A shoebox that rattled. Bread. He has laid none of them end to end, on purpose, the way you leave a present on the table and walk around it, and he isn’t going to start at midnight on a stairwell.

The screen has just gone over to 12:01 when feet come up from two, fast, slapping the concrete, taking the turn at the landing on one hand. Lena comes round the corner breathing hard from the hill: flour in her hair, flour on the knees of her jeans, the Saints sweatshirt with a brown scorch on one cuff in the shape of an oven rack, and on her hands, when she gets close, anise, and sugar, and the hot metal of the inside of an oven. She stops a step below him, so that she has to look up.
“It’s the nineteenth,” she says.

He looks at her — the flour, the scorch, the knot of hair she must have put up at seven and given up on by ten, the hill still going in and out of her — and can’t think of one smart thing to say, which hasn’t happened to him on these stairs since November.

She takes his face in both her floury hands and kisses him, quick, the way you’d stamp a thing to say it’s been seen to — and then not quick at all. She tastes of sugar and anise, and her cheek is cold from Ocean Road, and her mouth isn’t. He has the RAZR in one hand and nothing in the other and puts the empty one on the back of her sweatshirt, where it’s warm from running, and she leans up into him off the lower step, and the first kiss of his nineteenth year goes on long enough that the light over the door has time to flicker twice.
She ends it. Her thumbs stay on his cheekbones a second and leave flour there.
“You ran up the hill,” he says.
“I ran up the hill. Rudy timed me. He’s going to tell everybody eleven minutes. It was nine.” She’s still getting her breath. “I wanted to be first.”
“First what?”
“First anybody.”
Her hands have come down from his face, and she inspects the two pale thumbprints she’s left on him and seems satisfied with them.
“You burned your sweatshirt.”
She looks at the cuff as if it were somebody else’s. “The back of that oven runs hot. Everybody told me. I didn’t listen to everybody.”
“I have *dough* rising in a walk-in, Costigan.”

Ocean Road is a mile of hill each way. She ran up it for one minute on his stairs, and she is going to run back down it, at midnight, to bread he isn’t allowed to see. One foot is already on the step below.

choices.key: At one minute past midnight on your birthday, Lena came up the stairs with flour in her hair, and you thanked her.
response: “I haven’t done anything yet.”
“You did this.”

She opens her mouth to argue and doesn’t, which is new. At the turn she looks back up at him. “Go to *sleep*, Jack.” And she goes down the next flight at a run, one floury hand skidding on the rail, and leaves a white smear on it all the way down to two.

choices.text: “You’ve got a whole bakery in your hair.”
choices.key: At one minute past midnight on your birthday, Lena came up the stairs with flour in her hair, and you told her she had a whole bakery in it.
response: “I *am* a bakery. Go to sleep.”

She shakes her head at him, and flour comes down out of her hair onto his knee like the first snow on a Youngstown porch. At the turn of the stairs she stops and points up past him at the door to four, at 412 beyond it, until he holds up both hands and goes.

choices.text: “Nobody’s done midnight since I was a kid.”
choices.key: At one minute past midnight on your birthday, Lena came up the stairs with flour in her hair, and you told her nobody had done midnight for you since you were a kid.
response: She doesn’t answer. She comes back up the one step and kisses him on the forehead, like a blessing on a child going out the door, and goes.

He sits there with a print of flour on his forehead from her mouth, listening to her feet go all the way down and the lobby door after them, and then nothing but the tube light. He doesn’t wipe it off. He goes to bed with it.

s13.slug: FRIDAY · 6:41 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — 9:41 EASTERN
body: He has been awake since six with nowhere to be till noon, and couldn’t go back, and has come down to her landing in his socks the way he does, and her step is empty; the window over it is going from navy to the color of the inside of a shell, and down Ocean Road, he’d bet his tips, Rudy’s fryer has been on since five. He sits on her step anyway. When the RAZR goes the screen says GLENWOOD and 6:41, and he knows before he has it open: 9:41 Eastern, the minute he was born. Ma has called at it every year of his life, wherever he was — last year in the hall outside Latin at Mooney, with the second declension coming through the door — and he had forgotten she would.
“Seven pounds, eleven ounces,” Ma says, instead of hello. “Your father makes me say it. Happy birthday, sweetheart.”
“Hi, Ma.”

“Nineteen. I don’t know how that happened. I was there for all of it and I don’t know how.” A breath, Glenwood’s kitchen in it, the radio going on the windowsill. “I took the morning. Don’t tell anybody at St. Brigid’s I took it for this, they think I’m at the dentist.”

body.else: “The girl called me Monday,” she says. “Lena. She said to call her Lena.”

body: He opens his mouth.
“I’m not telling you what about. She’d kill me. I like her.”
“What did she —”
“What are you doing today?” Ma says, right over him.
“Mass at noon. I don’t know after that. Lena said —”

“Don’t tell me. I’m not supposed to know anything. I’m a school secretary, I know everything in that building and nothing in this one.” And, in the same breath: “Rosie mailed you something. I wasn’t allowed to see it. It went in an envelope with four stamps on it because she didn’t trust three.”

There is a click on the line, the extension in the front room coming off its hook, and breathing, and then Nonna, from Glenwood and eighty-four years away, loud, the way she talks to telephones: “*Auguri, Giacomino.*” And then something longer, fast, in the Calabrese he grew up under the table hearing and never learned, and in the middle of it he catches *fave* and nothing else.

“She says the girl has the beans,” Ma says. “She says that’s all she’ll say on a telephone.” Away from the receiver: “*Sì, Mà*, he heard you. The street heard you.” And to him, lower: “She’s been good this week. She’s had the calendar out on the table since Sunday. She knew what Friday was before I did.”

And Ma, quick and bright, the way she reads the lunch menu over the PA at St. Brigid’s: “When you were little Nonna did the table in the dining room. Danny was always Joseph. You were too little to be anything but the Bambino. You used to cry when they put you in the laundry basket.” And straight on, without a stop: “Is it nice out there? It’s sleeting. Your father’s out salting the steps like it’s January.”
“It’s nice,” Jack says. Over the landing the window has gone white with the morning.

A girl from three comes down past him in shower shoes with her caddy under her arm, and he pulls his knees in to let her by, and she mouths *sorry*, and he mouths *happy birthday* back at her by mistake, and she goes on down looking puzzled and pleased.
The RAZR buzzes against his ear while she’s telling him about the steps. He takes it away and looks.

body.text: HAPPY BIRTHDAY. 19. YOUR MOTHER SAYS I HAVE TO SAY THE WEIGHT. 7 LBS 11 OZ.

body: Each of them has blamed it on the other one. He can see it: his father on the front steps with a bag of rock salt under one arm, twenty feet from the phone in his mother’s hand, texting his son in capitals.
“Did he send it?” Ma says. “He’s been working on it since Tuesday.”
Ten minutes later, while Ma is telling him which of the Ferraro cousins got married and which only got engaged, it buzzes again.

body: “That’s your sister,” Ma says. “She’s supposed to be in chemistry.”

choices.text: “Thanks for calling at the minute, Ma.”
response: “Where else would I be at nine forty-one?”

And then she has to go; the dentist is expecting her at St. Brigid’s by half past ten. “Eat something,” she says. “I mean it. Something with a plate under it.” He sits on Lena’s step after she’s gone, in his socks, with the window over the landing all the way white and the day not started yet, and his own birthday in it.

choices.text: “Seven pounds eleven. I’ve been carrying it around.”
response: Ma laughs — the real one, from low down, the one he hasn’t heard since Christmas. On the extension Nonna wants to know what’s funny, and Ma tells her in Italian, and Nonna laughs too, a little behind, at the joke or at Ma, it doesn’t matter.
Jack holds the phone out from his ear on the stairwell to hear them better: the two of them laughing in a kitchen in Ohio, with the sleet on the window, at something he said.

choices.text: “I didn’t think anybody would do the table again.”
response: A pause on Glenwood. The radio on the windowsill fills it.
“Neither did I,” Ma says.
That’s all. And then: “Eat something.” And Jack, on a step in California, nods at a woman two thousand miles off who can’t see him do it, and keeps nodding.

s14.slug: FRIDAY · 12:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — WHITE
body: At twelve past nine, on the Hollis steps, his phone went.

body: He stood at the bottom of the steps with the RAZR open and people going round him on both sides, and after a while he wrote back.

At ten past twelve St. Brendan’s is white. Four weeks of purple and bare wood, and today Father Osei comes up the aisle in white and gold, and there are lilies on the flower stands either side of the altar where for a month there has been nothing but the stands, and the noon crowd — office people on their lunch hour, nursing students, two Knights, the woman with the walker, the Newman regulars in a clump near the front — looks up at it all like people who walked into the wrong church and are glad of it.

He has a clean shirt on under the Carhartt, the white one, ironed on Theo’s board. Lena is beside him in white lace. It’s her grandmother’s other veil, the one for feasts, and it makes her look like somebody he hasn’t met yet and would like to.

Up in the loft Gus, who has had four weeks of keeping it in, lets the Gloria out like a held breath — *Gloria in excelsis Deo* — the first since Ash Wednesday, and the noon crowd that doesn’t know the words sings anyway, and Lena beside him knows every one of them and sings them with her chin up, and Jack sings badly and doesn’t care who hears.

Father Osei reads Matthew. Joseph, a righteous man, finding her with child, and unwilling to expose her to shame; deciding to do it quietly; going to sleep on it; the angel in the dream — *do not be afraid* — and Joseph waking up and doing what he was told. That’s all Matthew gives him: no lines. Not one word out loud, not to her, not to the angel; he wakes up, and gets up, and does it. Jack has known men built that way, on the line at Lordstown and down the end of the bar at the K of C, and has always assumed they had nothing to say.

Father Osei closes the book and gives them two sentences. “Matthew calls Joseph a righteous man, and then tells us the righteous thing he had planned was to be quiet, and kind, and let nobody throw anything at her. Before any angel came, he had already decided that much on his own.”

They say the Creed, which nobody has said on a Friday since New Year’s Day, and the noon crowd stumbles into it. At *by the power of the Holy Spirit* Lena bows, and has hold of his elbow, and doesn’t seem to know she’s got it.

Afterward, in the courtyard, under the olive tree, the noon people go off to their cars and the sprinkler comes on over by the fence and somebody runs to turn it off. Lena takes the veil off and folds it. Father Osei goes by them toward the rectory with his vestments over his arm, looks once at Jack’s collar, says “Good,” and keeps going.
He opens the RAZR to the three texts and holds it out to her.
She reads them. All three, and his.
“That was kind of her.”
She closes the phone against her palm, carefully, so the cracked hinge won’t catch, and puts it back into his hand, and keeps her fingers on it a moment before she lets go.

body.text: She turns to her bag. “No fast today, Costigan. It’s a solemnity. Canon twelve fifty-one. I checked it twice and I asked a priest.” He had been going to keep bread and water till sundown. She has taken that off him like a coat at the door.
body.else: She turns to her bag. “No fish today, Costigan. It’s a solemnity. Canon twelve fifty-one. I checked it twice and I asked a priest.” He had been going to have the fish sticks at the Commons. She has taken that off him like a coat at the door.

body: “Which priest?”
“Father Osei. He laughed at me for a full minute, and then he said yes, and then he said I could have looked it up, and I said I *had*, twice.”

Out of the bag she brings a white bakery box tied with string, and out of the box, on a square of wax paper, a zeppola: a ring of fried dough, gold, split and piped full of cream, with a candied cherry sunk in the middle like a stone in a ring.
“Nonna’s recipe,” she says. “Rudy’s fryer. Five o’clock this morning. Rudy said the oil was too hot.” She lifts her chin. “Rudy was wrong.”
“You had one?”
“I ate the ugly ones at six. It’s a solemnity.”

He eats it standing under the olive tree at noon on a Friday in Lent. It is warm still at the center, and the cream has lemon peel in it, grated so fine you don’t see it, only taste it, and he knows on the first bite whose kitchen that came out of, and has to stop chewing a minute. She watches him eat it like a woman watching a fuse. “Is it right?” she says. “Tell me the truth. If the cream’s wrong I can go back down.” He can’t answer her with his mouth full, and then he can’t answer her for a different reason, and he nods instead, twice, and she looks down into the empty bakery box and says, “Good,” very quietly, to the box. Sugar comes off it down the front of the Carhartt, and she brushes it away with the back of her hand, brisk, the way her mother would brush down a child on the church steps, and doesn’t seem to notice she’s doing it. He eats the cherry last.
Lena takes the empty wax paper out of his hand and folds it into the box and the box into her bag, and walks backward three steps toward the gate, pointing at him.
“Five-thirty. The Fishbowl. Bring everybody you’ve ever met.”
